name: Earmuffs
summary: Hard cups with soft cushions that seal around the ears, on a headband or clipped to a hard hat; some have electronics that let quiet sounds through.
uses: Chainsaws, generators, grinders, compressors and engines: easier to fit well than plugs, but still less than the label
Quick on and off for noise that comes and goes; easy to see and grab, and easy with dirty or gloved hands
At 100 dBA and up, or for sudden loud bangs, NIOSH says wear muffs over plugs; CCOHS counts the pair as only 5 dB better than the higher rating (NIOSH bulletin; CCOHS hearing)
The seal leaks over thick glasses arms, hats, hoods and long hair, and cushions stop sealing in hard cold
Too much protection hides alarms and shouts; aim to hear voices, not the roar
identify: Two hard cups with soft cushions that press round the ears, joined by a headband or attached to a hard hat (NIOSH hearing PPE). Some cushions are filled with liquid (EC hearing protection). US muffs carry an NRR on the package (OSHA OTM). Canadian ones may show a class under CSA Z94.2: A for about 95–105 dBA, B for 90–95, C for below 90 (WorkSafeBC hearing; WorkplaceNL hearing). European muffs fall under EN 352-1, or EN 352-3 if made to attach to a helmet, and should carry the CE mark; the figures used to choose them are the SNR and the H, M and L values; electronic level-dependent and radio muffs come under the same family (DIN EN 352-1; uvex EN 352; OSHWIKI hearing). Lab numbers run high: NIOSH takes 25% off a muff's NRR, CSA Z94.2 uses 70% of it, OSHA takes 7 dB off for dBA readings and halves the rest to judge engineering controls, and HSE says to assume the level at the ear is 4 dB higher than the standard test predicts (NIOSH 98-126; CCOHS hearing; OSHA OTM; HSE real world). A helmet and muff that clip together are not proof they protect together (HSE press 2025). Music headphones are never hearing protection (NIOSH 98-126). No rating anywhere: treat it as unknown.
test: Look it over: cups uncracked, cushions soft and whole with no splits or hard, flattened patches, the foam inserts still inside the cups, and a headband that still squeezes firmly. Stretched headbands, missing foam, damaged seals and cracked cups give false security (HSE press 2025; HSE hearing protection). A damaged liquid cushion will leak (EC hearing protection). Replace cushions that are no longer pliable, and replace the muff when the band is so stretched the cushions no longer sit snug (CCOHS hearing). Honeywell says to replace snap-in cushions and foam inserts every 6 months, or more often with heavy use (Honeywell hygiene kits). Don't bend the headband to change the fit (EC hearing protection). To fit: pull hair back, take off caps and hoods, put the cups fully over the ears and slide them until the cushions seal all round (CCOHS hearing; HSE hearing protection; HSE press 2025). In one maker's test, glasses arms 2 mm thick or less made no significant difference; 3 mm arms cost about 2 dB of NRR and 6 mm arms about 5 dB, and one pair of 6 mm arms lost 9–12 dB at some pitches (Honeywell eyewear). In very cold weather the cushions don't seal well (NIOSH hearing PPE).

decay.note: Estimate. Honeywell says to replace snap-in cushions and foam inserts every 6 months, or more often with heavy use. Cushions that stop being pliable, and bands stretched so the cushions don't sit snug, are reasons to replace the muff (CCOHS hearing).

improvise: Earplugs are the other kind of hearing protector (NIOSH hearing PPE), and NIOSH says to wear muffs over plugs at 100 dBA and above (NIOSH bulletin). A muff with cracked, hard or missing cushions leaks and gives false security (HSE press 2025); if you find a hygiene kit of cushions for that model, fit it (Honeywell hygiene kits). Music headphones and earbuds are not hearing protection (NIOSH 98-126). Motorcycle helmets are quite acoustically leaky and cotton gives only about 5–10 dB except at the highest pitches (Berger 2006); NIOSH says cotton should not be used in place of hearing protectors (NIOSH 98-126). For a brief blast, fingers pushed firmly into the ear canals give about 25–30 dB, but you can't work like that (Berger 2006). Otherwise, get away from the noise and cut the time near it (NIOSH 98-126). Store muffs hanging by the headband; when they are clipped to a hard hat, don't leave the cushions pressed against the shell, which flattens them (WorkplaceNL hearing).
